name: SWE-Gym
description: SWE-Gym is the first training environment for software engineering agents, containing 2,438 real-world task instances from 11 popular Python repositories. Each instance comprises a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The environment enables training of language model-based SWE agents and verifiers with executable feedback.
citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. ICML 2025.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym comprises 2,438 real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. The dataset construction involved: (1) Identifying repositories using SEART GitHub search with filters for Python repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories; (2) Extracting training instances from repositories using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including natural language description, repository snapshot, and unit tests, resulting in 64,689 task instances (SWE-Gym Raw); (3) Version training instances by associating instances with version numbers and setting up environments version-by-version; (4) Setup executable environments and verify instances by manually configuring dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation, requiring approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours, resulting in 2,438 unit-test-validated instances from 11 repositories.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues and pull requests from 11 popular Python repositories (pandas, MONAI, moto, mypy, dvc, dask, modin, pydantic, conan, hydra, bokeh). The raw data includes natural language descriptions of issues, snapshots of repositories at the time of issue creation, and associated unit tests. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 task instances spanning 358 Python repositories.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The preprocessing involved: (1) Filtering repositories based on criteria (Python, created before July 1, 2022, >500 stars, >300 lines of code, >500 PRs, >100 contributors); (2) Extracting task instances using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script; (3) Versioning instances by associating them with version numbers; (4) Manually configuring dependencies for each task instance using configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation; (5) Using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than original code; (6) Filtering out failed instances after validation. For SWE-Gym Lite (230 instances), additional filtering excluded tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset uses expert-written unit tests from the original GitHub repositories as evaluation signals. Human annotations were performed to manually configure dependencies for each task instance, requiring approximately 200 human annotation hours. The annotations involved examining configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, and documentation from repository snapshots to ensure executable environments with pre-installed dependencies.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Validation was performed using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch (human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. This process involved 10,000 CPU core hours of computation. Failed instances were filtered out after validation.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors (researchers from UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, and Apple).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script, SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors publicly release SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories. Pre-built Docker images for each instance are released, totaling 6 TB. The paper mentions SWE-Gym Raw as a resource for future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The work presents implications for automated software engineering capabilities that could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. The authors note that improving automated software engineering could support critical open-source infrastructure and make software development more accessible. However, they also acknowledge potential impacts on software engineering jobs and considerations around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. The authors note that while they focus on legitimate software engineering tasks, similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code.
rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total tasks while bokeh represents only one percent. The authors note that tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those in SWE-Bench, with gold patches having significantly more lines and files edited. The dataset is limited to Python repositories and may not generalize to other programming languages. The manual environment configuration process may introduce bias away from tasks with complex dependencies. The authors also note that repeated sampling shows task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, where the dataset introduces bias toward easier tasks.
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). Codebases in SWE-Gym have relatively fewer files than SWE-Bench on average, though similar total lines of code. The dataset construction required substantial manual effort (approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours). Models have consistently lower performance on SWE-Gym compared to SWE-Bench, which may be due to the inclusion of sophisticated repositories like pandas and MONAI. The authors note that current performance is limited by compute budget for sampling rather than the number of tasks in SWE-Gym. The dataset focuses solely on task completion and neglects human-in-the-loop collaboration essential for real-world software engineering.
rai:dataUseCases: Training: SWE-Gym is designed for training language model-based software engineering agents and verifiers. The environment enables supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning approaches. Testing/Validation: The dataset includes executable environments with unit tests for evaluating agent performance. The authors use SWE-Bench Lite and SWE-Bench Verified as separate test sets for evaluation. Use cases include: (1) Training SWE agents using general-purpose prompting scaffolds (OpenHands) and specialized workflow scaffolds (MoatlessTools); (2) Training verifier models for inference-time scaling; (3) Self-improvement through iterative rejection sampling fine-tuning; (4) Research in automatic environment synthesis, reinforcement learning for agents, and human-agent interaction.
